speaker: adamsudbury
text: Thank you, Your Honor. May it please the court. My name is Adam Sudbury. I represent Tania Torriella and Luxury Living Developers Corporation. As is stated correctly in the appellee's brief, Luxury Living Developers Corporation has abandoned its appeal in this case. This case relates back to a mortgage loan from 2009. Very briefly, the procedural history of the case is that there were numerous attempts to obtain personal jurisdiction by service of process over the plaintiffs that all failed over the course of 10 years. Ultimately, the court entered final judgment under rule 1.070J dismissing the case for that failure. Ms. Torriella filed a motion of tax, attorney's fees and costs, and that matter was decided against her in the lower tribunal. We've now appealed to this court to address that collateral claim. I would like to, unless the court has any specific questions about our argument to establish the attorney's fee claim, I would like to spend the balance of my time here addressing some of the arguments raised in the answer brief. Specifically, the appellee raises two arguments in its answer brief. First, that Ms. Torriella cannot be considered the prevailing party, and therefore fees cannot be awarded on that basis. And second, that Ms. Torriella has a bankruptcy discharge that converts the mortgage and the note into non-recourse instruments, and therefore cannot be awarded attorney's fees under a certain case law that applies to non-recourse instruments. I'd like to start with the second argument, and Ms. Torriella would argue that the plaintiff has impermissibly gone outside of the record on appeal in order to make that argument. There are only two places in the record on appeal, both cited in the answer brief, that they can point to as any factual support for this position. The first place that they point to is at the record, page 207, in an affidavit where Ms. Torriella states, quote, I did file bankruptcy in 2010 with the Middle District of Florida, and cites a case number. And then they point to the underlying plaintiffs on affidavit called the Affidavit of Diligent Search and Inquiry that reflects a bankruptcy search conducted in support of that affidavit. And they state in that affidavit that there was a bankruptcy discharge. The problem with those two places in the record are number one, an underlying affidavit is hearsay within hearsay as to that specific point in contention and can't be considered substantive evidence in support of that position. And number two, Ms. Torriella merely stated that she filed bankruptcy, which does not establish any form of bankruptcy discharge. There is nothing else in the record. There's no judgment in the record on appeal reflecting a bankruptcy discharge or what the terms of that discharge may or may not have been. And therefore the plaintiff, or I should say the appellee, should not be permitted in this court to go outside of that record in order to establish this argument. The second point that they raised, which is really their first point in their brief, is that Ms. Torriella is not the prevailing party and therefore should not be permitted to recover attorney's fees under 57-105 subsection seven. There is no dispute that there are two provisions in these instruments that allow recovery of attorney's fees or at least allow the plaintiff to recover, or the appellee to recover its attorney's fees. That is in the promissory note at paragraph seven subsection E, which states if the note holder has required me to pay in full, et cetera, et cetera, they will have the right to be paid back by me for all of its costs and expenses and enforcing this note to the extent not prohibited by law. Those expenses include, for example, reasonable attorney's fees. And then paragraph 22 of the mortgage towards the end of the paragraph, it states lender, referring to the appellee or its successors, shall be entitled to collect all expenses incurred in pursuing the remedies provided in this section 22, including, but not limited to, reasonable attorney's fees and cost of title evidence. The reason I point specifically to the language of the two paragraphs is because when the court is determining whether or not to grant attorney's fees under 57-105 subsection seven, it needs to look specifically to the provisions of the contract and what that contract says about-

text: Yes, thank you. Good morning, Your Honors. Eric Levine on behalf of NationStar Mortgage LLC. May it please the court. A lot of dismissal, as the American Home Assurance Court said, a dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction does not convert prevailing party status on any party. It's legally impossible with that discharge in place. 57-105 was designed to even the playing field. Every party has the same rights. So Ms. Torella, armed with a bankruptcy discharge, says the bank can't get their fees against me, but I wanna get it against them. That's not permissible. That goes beyond what 57-105 was designed to do, and I'll use a colloquial, what's good for the goose is good for the gander. If she has no problem discharging her personal liability under these loan documents for any attorney's fees we incur, she has to recognize that any personal liability the bank might have for her fees is also discharged. However, those federal courts, the cases that he has cited, that the appellee has cited, are not directly on point, and they discuss statutes that award attorney's fees, such as under unfair and deceptive trade practices, Uniform Trade Secrets Act. And the one case that is somewhat analogous is Religious Technology Center versus Liebrich. This is 98 Federal Appendix 978, where that court, in considering the argument, pointed very directly and specifically to the provisions of the contract, making it clear that it is very important to do exactly that and to refer back to the contract and to read exactly what the contract says about the fees that are allowed to either party when deciding whether it can be shifted under 57-105. So in that case, the reason that it was denied was because the contract stated specifically that it required a breach of the agreement to be established and that under the circumstances in that case, there was no breach that could be pointed to or established in the case in order to trigger that provision. What we believe is most analogous under that prevailing party language to this case is the jurisprudence out of this court and other Florida courts that state that a voluntary dismissal is a determination for purposes of prevailing party to recover attorney's fees under 57-105 Subsection 7. And the reason why it's most analogous and the court should really look at the voluntary dismissal jurisprudence is because a voluntary dismissal when one is taken, especially in a mortgage foreclosure action, operates as an adjudication, not on the merits, but they can take one without prejudice. So it is a dismissal without prejudice in the same way that a 1.070 dismissal is without prejudice. So a voluntary dismissal-
